slides.title: A word at the start
slides.text:
Some sentences start with one **opening word**.

**First**, wash your hands.
**Yes**, I can help.
**Suddenly**, the lights went out.

slides.title: Add a comma
slides.text:
Put a **comma** right after the opening word.

The comma tells the reader to take a tiny **pause**.

**Finally,** we went home.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Look at the first word of the sentence.
2. Is it an opening word like First or Yes?
3. Find other sentences in the text that start the same way. See where their commas go.

example.explain: **First**, **Next** and **Finally** are opening words. Each one has a comma right after it.

together.passage: Yesterday was my birthday. First, Mom made a big cake. Next, my cousins came over. We played games in the yard.
together.stem: Which is the best last sentence for the story?
together.hint: Look at the other sentences that start with an opening word. Where do their commas go?
together.good: Yes! The comma goes right after the opening word **Finally**.

sentences: First, Mom made a big cake.
We played games in the yard.
evidence.stem: The answer was: Finally, we ate the cake. Tap 2 sentences that also have a comma after an opening word.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not start with an opening word. Find sentences with First or Next.

checks.passage: ___ I can come to your house.
checks.stem: Which word and comma fill the blank?
checks.why: **Yes** is an opening word, so a comma comes right after it.

checks.passage: Suddenly the cat jumped on the table.
checks.why: **Suddenly** is an opening word. The comma goes right after it.

checks.passage: No, thank you. Well I am not hungry.
checks.stem: Which word needs a comma after it?
checks.why: **Well** is an opening word, so it needs a comma: **Well,** I am not hungry.

again.title: Clap and pause
again.text: Read the sentence out loud. Clap once after the opening word. That clap is your **comma**.
again.example:
Luckily (clap) it stopped raining.

**Luckily,** it stopped raining.

slides.title: Opening words
slides.text:
Put a comma after an opening word:

**Yes,** I finished.
**However,** the shop was closed.

Also use a comma when you **talk to someone by name**:
**Huda,** please pass the bread.

slides.title: Opening phrases
slides.text:
A **phrase** is a small group of words. When a phrase opens the sentence, put a comma after it.

**After lunch,** we went outside.
**In the morning,** the market is busy.

slides.title: Find the main part
slides.text:
The comma separates the **opening** from the **main part** of the sentence.

**At the end of the day,** | **we went home.**

The main part has the subject and the verb.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find where the opening word or phrase ends.
2. Find where the main part (subject + verb) starts.
3. The comma goes between them.

Other sentences in the passage that follow this pattern are your proof.

sentences.t: During the holiday, we visited our grandparents.

example.explain:
**During the holiday** is an opening phrase. **Yes** is an opening word. Each is followed by a comma, then the main part.

The last sentence has no opening part, so it needs no comma.

together.passage: Our class went to the aquarium in Jeddah. In the first room, we saw hundreds of colourful fish. Yes, there was even a shark! Later, a guide showed us how sea turtles are cared for.
options: At the end, of the visit we bought postcards.
At the end of the visit we, bought postcards.
At, the end of the visit we bought postcards.
At the end of the visit, we bought postcards.
together.hint: Find where the opening phrase ends and the main part (we bought) begins.
together.good: Yes! **At the end of the visit** is the opening phrase, so the comma goes before **we bought**.

sentences: Our class went to the aquarium in Jeddah.
In the first room, we saw hundreds of colourful fish.
Yes, there was even a shark!
Later, a guide showed us how sea turtles are cared for.
evidence.stem: The answer was: At the end of the visit, we bought postcards. Tap 2 sentences that also use a comma after an opening word or phrase.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not start with an opening word or phrase. Look for one that does.

checks.passage: After the football match we ate dinner.
checks.why: **After the football match** is the opening phrase, so the comma goes after **match**.

checks.passage: Salma can you help me carry this box?
checks.why: We are talking to Salma by name, so put a comma after **Salma**.

checks.passage: Which sentence uses a comma correctly?
options: On Friday we, visited the beach.
On, Friday we visited the beach.
On Friday, we visited the beach.
On Friday we visited, the beach.
checks.why: **On Friday** is the opening phrase. The comma goes right after it.

again.title: Find the who
again.text: Find the **who** in the sentence (the subject). Put the comma just **before** it.
again.example:
In the evening we read stories.

Who? **we**. Put the comma before it:
**In the evening, we read stories.**

slides.title: Opening clauses
slides.text:
A **clause** has its own subject and verb. Some clauses cannot stand alone. They start with words like **when, if, because, after, before, while, although**.

**When the bell rang**, the students lined up.

slides.title: Comma after, not before
slides.text:
When the clause comes **first**, put a comma after it.
**If you finish early,** you may read.

When the clause comes **last**, you usually need **no** comma.
You may read **if you finish early**.

slides.title: Words, phrases, clauses
slides.text:
Word: **However,** the shop was closed.
Phrase: **Near the old well,** we found a coin.
Clause: **Because it was late,** we walked quickly.

All three opening parts take a comma.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Does the sentence **begin** with when, if, because, after, although?
2. Find where that clause ends and the main clause begins.
3. Put the comma there.

Compare with other sentences in the passage. Notice which ones open with a clause, and which ones put it at the end.

sentences.t: Although it was very hot, the children kept playing.
They drank water whenever they felt tired.
Before the sun set, everyone went home.

example.explain:
Sentences 1 and 3 **open** with a clause, so they need a comma.

In sentence 2 the clause **whenever they felt tired** comes at the **end**, so no comma is needed.

together.passage: When the power went out last night, our street became very dark. Because the fridge stopped working, Mom moved the milk into a cool box. My little brother was scared until Dad lit a lamp. If the power had stayed off longer we would have gone to Grandma's house. Luckily, it came back after two hours.
together.stem: Which sentence is missing a comma?
options: When the power went out last night, our street became very dark.
My little brother was scared until Dad lit a lamp.
If the power had stayed off longer we would have gone to Grandma's house.
Luckily, it came back after two hours.
together.hint: Which sentence opens with a clause (if, when, because) but has no comma after it?
together.good: Yes! **If the power had stayed off longer** is an opening clause, so it needs a comma before **we**.

sentences: When the power went out last night, our street became very dark.
Because the fridge stopped working, Mom moved the milk into a cool box.
My little brother was scared until Dad lit a lamp.
If the power had stayed off longer we would have gone to Grandma's house.
Luckily, it came back after two hours.
evidence.stem: The answer was the sentence beginning 'If the power had stayed off longer'. Tap 2 sentences that show the correct pattern: an opening clause, then a comma.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not show the pattern. Its clause comes at the end, it opens with just one word, or its comma is missing.

checks.passage: Before you leave the classroom please push in your chair.
checks.why: **Before you leave the classroom** is the opening clause, so the comma goes after **classroom**.

options: We stayed inside, because it was raining.
Because it was raining we, stayed inside.
Because, it was raining we stayed inside.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
checks.why: The clause **Because it was raining** opens the sentence, so a comma follows it. When the clause comes last, no comma is needed.

checks.passage: While Grandma told stories, we sat on the carpet and listened.
checks.stem: Why does this sentence have a comma?
options: It separates an opening clause from the main clause.
It comes before the word and.
checks.why: **While Grandma told stories** is an opening clause. The comma separates it from the main clause **we sat**.

again.title: Opening clause = waiting
again.text: An opening clause makes the reader **wait** for the main idea. The comma marks the end of the waiting.
again.example:
If it rains tomorrow ... (what?) → we will stay home.

**If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.**

slides.title: Opening verbal phrases
slides.text:
Phrases built on **-ing** or **-ed** verb forms often open a sentence. Put a comma after them.

**Hoping to win,** the team trained daily.
**Tired after the long trip,** we went straight to bed.

slides.title: Long and stacked phrases
slides.text:
Several prepositional phrases in a row also take a comma.

**On the first day of the holiday,** we drove to Abha.

After a very **short** phrase, the comma is sometimes optional: **In 2020** we moved. But a comma is never wrong there.

slides.title: Comma to stop misreading
slides.text:
Sometimes a comma prevents confusion.

Confusing: While we were eating the cat jumped on the table.
Clear: While we were eating, the cat jumped on the table.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the opening element: word, phrase or clause.
2. Find the subject of the main clause.
3. The comma belongs right before that subject.

Other sentences in the passage that place the comma the same way support your answer.

sentences.t: Climbing the steep path, the hikers breathed hard.
At the top of the hill near the old tower, they rested.
The view was worth the effort.

example.explain:
**Climbing the steep path** is a verbal phrase. **At the top of the hill near the old tower** is a stack of phrases. Each is followed by a comma, then the subject.

The last sentence opens with its subject, so no comma is needed.

together.passage: Hoping to see the sunrise, the hikers left their camp before dawn. The trail up the mountain was steep and rocky. Near the top of the ridge above the valley, they stopped to catch their breath. Tired but determined the youngest hiker kept climbing without a word. The group reached the summit just as the sun rose over the peaks.
together.stem: In the sentence beginning 'Tired but determined', where should a comma be added?
together.hint: Find the subject of the main clause. The opening phrase ends just before it.
together.good: Yes! **Tired but determined** is the opening phrase, and **the youngest hiker** is the subject. The comma goes after **determined**.

sentences: Hoping to see the sunrise, the hikers left their camp before dawn.
The trail up the mountain was steep and rocky.
Near the top of the ridge above the valley, they stopped to catch their breath.
Tired but determined the youngest hiker kept climbing without a word.
The group reached the summit just as the sun rose over the peaks.
evidence.stem: The answer was: after determined. Tap 2 sentences that correctly use a comma after an opening phrase.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not show the pattern: it starts with its subject, or its comma is missing. Find an opening phrase followed by a comma.

checks.passage: Excited by the news the students cheered loudly.
checks.why: **Excited by the news** is an opening verbal phrase, so the comma goes after **news**, before the subject.

checks.passage: After eating the children went out to play.
checks.stem: Why does this sentence need a comma after 'eating'?
options: Because the sentence is a question.
Without it, a reader might think someone ate the children.
checks.why: The comma prevents misreading: **After eating, the children went out to play.**

options: Running to catch the bus, Majed dropped his book.
Running to catch, the bus Majed dropped his book.
Running, to catch the bus Majed dropped his book.
Running to catch the bus Majed, dropped his book.
checks.why: **Running to catch the bus** is the opening phrase. The comma goes before the subject **Majed**.

again.title: Comma before the subject
again.text: In almost every case, the comma after an opening part sits **right before the subject** of the main clause.
again.example:
Covered in dust the old book sat on the shelf.

Subject: **the old book**. Comma before it:
**Covered in dust, the old book sat on the shelf.**
